Pigeons Feel the Pinch London, June pigeons of St<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Paul&#x27;s are not as fat as they used to be. War rations and airraids have affected he them materially. Visitors to London&#x27;s famous cathedral are not as numerous as they were in pre- war days and even those persons who do feed the pigeons now days don&#x27;t care to pay twenty-five cents a pint for peanuts just to see the big birds peck. It&#x27;s a violation of Defense of the Realm Act to feed bread to birds, so the pigeons have to content themselves principally with scanty leavings from the cab horses&#x27; dinner bags. The pigeons of St<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Paul&#x27;s, and of all London, too, dread the buzz of an airplane propeller overhead and even during the daytime when an observing allied aviator appears in the sky--and this is almost daily--the pigeons flutter about and fret considerably until he is out of sight. And at night, when the Boches have come, dropping bombs and things, the pigeons are out in a jiffy from their roost in the belfry wherein is hung Great Paul of seventeen tons, St. Paul&#x27;s largest bell, never returning until daylight. They spend the remainder of the night on adjoining buildings or wherever they happen to alight when the air raid is at ite height. &quot;One could feed those pigeons all the peanuts and wheat they could eat,&quot; said a policeman, whose station is near St<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Paul&#x27;s Cathedral, recently, &quot;but they&#x27;ll never take on any flesh so long a8 there are aviators about. Bombs and the hum of the airplane worry them nearly out of their feathers.&quot; Lake Resorts in Southern B.C. &quot;Lake Resorts in Southern British Columbia&quot; is a new and handsomely illustrated folder just issued by the Canadian Pacific Railway. South of the main line of the C.P.R. through the Rocky Mountains, stretching to the U<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">S. border, is a wonderful district that is comparatively little known. It is extremely picturesque, its lakes, mountain peaks, fruit orchards and metal mines offering a variety of interest. With the construction of the Kettle Valley Railway, it is now possible to reach Vancouver by this southern route, leaving the main line of the C.P.R. at Medicine Hat, and traversing the Crow&#x27;s Nest Pass, Kootenay Lake, passing the Arrow Lakes and Okanagan Lake, and thence to Vancouver through the Coquihalla Canyon<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">This district, which is well served by both rail and water transportation, 18 becoming a popular holiday resort as well as a different route through to the Pacific Coast; and the C.P.R., in order to give information about the many beautiful places en route, have issued this folder. Amongst the districts described are the Columbia Valley, Kootenay Lake. Nelson, Kaslo, the Arrow Lakes, Nakusp, the Slocan Lake, Okanagan Lake, Penticton. Kelowna, etc. Copies of the folder can be obtained from Mr<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">F. C. Lydon, City Passenger Agent, 141- 145 St. James Montreal. GERMAN OFFICIAL Fighting Activity Revived in Kemmel Region Berlin, via London, July official communication from general headquarters today says: &quot;In the Kemmel region, on the Lys and on the Somme, fighting activity revived in the evening<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">The French have kept up their violent partial attacks. &quot;Southwest of and south of the Aisne they advanced several times with strong forces and lished themselves in the farms of Porte and Des Loges, west of Antheufl as well as in old French trenches north of Longpont. On the adjoining sectors they were repulsed by our fire. captured prisoners in a successful local assault west of Chateau Thierry. There has been lively reconnoitering activity by the enemy on both sides of Rheims, Storming troops brought back prisoners from French trenches north of Largitzen.&quot; Sydney Dispute Settled pute, J<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">announced to78 night Mr. Watters&#x27; had nothing street, further to state on the labor situation Mount here. The Sydney, N.S, July moulders and the Dominion Coal and Steel Company have settled their labor disC. Watters RAIDS BY POLICE NET 250 PERSONS Surprise Visit Also Resulted in Seizure of 32 Slot Machines CAREFULLY PLANNED Raiding Parties Visited Suspected Premises Simultaneously Search Warrants Used The first 1 big gun in Director Joseph Tremblay&#x27;s effort with the Montreal police to clean the city of vice was fired last night when two big raids planned, organized and carried out by the Director of Public Sofetly, the Assistant, Arthur Mann, and Deputy Chief of Police Grandchamps, landed nearly two hundred and fifty men and women in the police net. Both raids were worked on the same plan the men entering all the places on the list at the same time, and on each occasion the police were successful<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">In the first raid thirtytwo slot machines were seized, and in the second nearly two hundred and fifty men and women were taken. The first raid was timed for 9.30 o&#x27;clock, and the list of all the places where slot machines were located had been furnished the leaders, who, with their men, waited for the strikIng of the clock before they entered simultaneously twenty-three clubs, cigar stores and places of amusement. The proprietors of the places had apparently some wind of the affair, and for the most part acted as though surprised, but said that they did not have any machines on their premises. The police, armed with search warrants, scoured the premises and generally machines were brought to light. Some of machines were found at their regular stands, others were discovered in the cellars, storerooms housed some, and one or two machines had been hidden under the roof of the house<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">The machines, totalling 32, were taken to headquarters and placed in the office of the Director of Public Safety until there was hardly room to move about in the office. The machines, the total value of which is placed at $3,350, contained plenty of money found in the machines. It was stated last night that the machines would be used first as evidence in the court today and will later be destroyed. Only one man was held by the police in the raid, but all the owners and users of the machines were summoned to appear in court on a charge of gambling. The machines are gum vending machines and in most cases there was, the police state, no gum in the machines<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">The police had received several complaints about the machines lately, and it was these complaints that decided the officials to act so promptly. After a few days of hard work the detectives secured the addresses of all the stores having the machines and these were all raided last night. RAID AT MIDNIGHT. At twelve o&#x27;clock, raid of another nature was made in fifteen alleged houses of ill-fame, which cleared nearly 250 prisoners. About seventy-five p.c<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">of the prisoners were women. The men, as in the previous raid, entered the places at the&#x27; same time and prevented the alarm from being raised and the completeness of the raid spoiled. In all of the houses several women and men were found, and all were taken to headquarters. Very few of the prisoners were allowed out on bail and these few were men. Nearly every nationality was represented in the captures<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Negroes and a Chinaman were among them. There, were also several soldiers in During the two raids all the patrol waggons of the city were used, in addition to seven automobiles and some twenty cabs. Seventy-five men, who had done duty all day, under captains of the various stations, and the inspectors, took part in the raids, which were said to be the biggest of their kind evor made in Montreal. The organization was perfect and in not a single Instance was there a hitch. The first raid took place at 9.30 and an hour afterwards the machines were all in the headquarters office to be checked up and made ready to produce as evidence in the morning<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">In the second raid more rigs were wanted and the various waggons had to make several trips. Early this morning the waggons were still arriving with prisoners. The two raids were planned Director Tremblay and, seconded by Assistant Director Mann and Deputy Chief Grandchamps, the work went well. Orders were given to the detectives and the policemen and their officers of the day staff only at 5 o&#x27;clock in order to make the raids as complete a surprise as possible. Most of the streets of the Red Light district were visited in the second raid, while in the first various sections of the city were cleaned up<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">All the prisoners and those summoned will appear in the arraignment court today, charged either with gambling, keeping gambling houses, and being in houses of illfame, or keeping disorderly houses. A quantity of liquor was seized in the second raid. Director of. Publid Safety Joseph Tremblay stated this morning after the second raid that the underworld must now realize that there is a new administration. &quot;The lid is on,&quot; said Mr<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Tremblay, &quot;and we will endeavor to keep it on tight.&quot; A Long and Fast Run (Oxbow, Herald.) We have heard tell of people, even in this country, being chased by dog or a bull, but George Robson had an unusual experience one day last week with a rattlesnake. which, for real down right excitement, knocks common everyday occurrences higher than a cocked hat. Space forbids us giving the details of Mr. Robson&#x27;s encounter with this venomous reptile, suffice to say that he is not yet fully recovered from the scare he received and the long run he made to escape its poisonous sting. This snake was not seen, but the weird rattle which these reptiles extend in times of charge was quite sufficient for the pursued to make his presence scarce<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">LIFE ON U.S. TROOPSHIPS Menace Chief Submarine, Men on Board London, June 6-(Correspondence of The Associated Press) Although troopships that bring over American soldiers are 80 well protected that the submarine menace is virtually negligible, submarines throughout the trip are probably the chief subject of conversation. Usually the references to the undersea terror are jocular, but it is apparent that much serious thought is given to U-boats and that they loom large in imagination. This applies to officers as well as to the men. All say frankly they have no desire for a brush with the slinking, enemy craft<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">The reason for this was neatly put by a major of infantry, who recently landed in England. &quot;Fighting submarines,&quot; he said, &quot;isn&#x27;t our game.&quot; In that pithy explanation he summed up the soldiers&#x27; attitude exactly. Fighting the submarines isn&#x27;t the army&#x27;s game, and soldiers can&#x27;t play it because they don&#x27;t know how. If their ship is attacked there is nothing for them to do except march on deck and prepare to take to the lifeboats. Defensive measures rest with the transport&#x27;s naval guns and with the escorting destroyers<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">They, as the soldier sees it, have all the fun, while the soidier must stand by, eager to fight, but helpless to take a hand. The army officers feel keenly their responsibility in such an unfamiliar situation. It devolves upon them to clear the ship of every man and get them into their proper boats. In order to do this with the greatest celerity and precision, the commanding military officer and his assistants carefully work out their plans before the ship sails. On a large vessel carrying several thousand troops, it is necessary to quarter the men on all decks, some far down in the vessel<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">The task, then, is to get them all up on the boat deck with the least delay and without confusion. Boat drills begin soon after the ship leaves port. Each man is assigned to a particular boat, and it is highly important that when the troops, in response to the alarm signal, are moving up from the lower decks that there be no interference and congestion on the stairways. The problem presents a 1 number of difficulties, each of which is studied with care. So perfect was the system employed on one big transport<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">that the 6,000 troops on board could be brought from all parts of the ship to their stations on the upper deck within less than five minutes. When a transport approaches the submarine zone, precautions are increased. All officers and men must wear their life-preservers constantly, and when the ship has got well into the zone, orders are issued for the men to sleep in their clothes. No lights, of course, are shown. To guard against the inadvertent striking of a match, whose flare might reveal the vessel&#x27;s presence to a lurking submarine, no one is permitted on deck after dark, with the exception of the ship&#x27;s crew<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Sentries are posted to see that this order is strictly obeyed. An amusing incident occurred on a huge British transport which was carrying a particularly large number of American soldiers. About nine o&#x27;clock one evening, while full speed was being made through the heart of the zone, a sentry noticed a ray of light playing in a small circle on a distant part of the deck which he was guarding. He called another sentry and together they crept toward the point where the light momentarily had appeared. The night was very dark and at first the sentries could see nothing<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Then they made out the figure of a man bending over the deck. They immediately seized him and told him he was under arrst. &quot;But I&#x27;m the watch officer in command of the ship,&quot; the prisoner exclaimed. &quot;I have to use a flashlight for the work I&#x27;m doing here.&quot; However, the sentries had their orders. They were to arrest anybody that showed a light on deck<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">So their captive protested in vain. The soldiers called their officer of the day. He decided i to turn the prisoner over to the ship&#x27;s captain. Up to the bridge the watch officer was taken, and when the captain saw him and heard the details, he almost choked with laughter. It will be a long time before that officer is permitted to forget his arrest on his own ship by American soldiers<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">ENEMIES OF RUSSIA Bolsheviki and Huns Allied, With Late Mirbach Dictator London Times Cable Service, Copy- right, 1918. Stockholm, July Nyheter publishes today a letter from Terestchenko, former foreign minister in the Kerensky Government, to Burtzeff, the revolutionary leader, now in France, which, although written before Terestchenko left Russia to join his chief in England, throws light on the position and part played by the late Count Mirbach, German representative at Moscow, and the all-powerful influence he had with the Bolshevik Government when his career was so tragically ended. He says: &quot;There reigns now in Moscow a proconsul whose name is Mirbach. Bolsheviki eloquence flows as usual, but ceases immediately at a frown of this gentleman&#x27;s brow. Lenine and Trotzky govern Moscow only thanks to him<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">It would be the easiest thing for the Germans to turn them out, but they know better. The Bolsheviki are more useful to them even than a government composed of their own generals. Is it not a curious fact while friendly Ukraine Germans and Austrians are obliged to keep an army in the rest of Russia, the Germans require no troops at all, thanks to the Bolsheviki, who do all they can for them. Their wishes are carried out promptly as they would be by their own well-disciplined people. Germany will not permit the reorganization of Russia even with her aid until peace is concluded.&quot; After describing at length the present condition of Russia resulting from &quot;fourteen months of revolution and six months of Bolshevik dominion.&quot; the writer concludes that Russia has two enemies, the Bolsheviki and the Germans, and at present they are allied<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">PERSONAL INTELLIGENCE Mr. Shunsoka Noda, of New York, is at the Place Viger. NAVY LEAGUE HAD TWO BIG MEETINGS Demonstrations For EnglishSpeaking People Held in Lafontaine Park &quot;SCOUT SHIP&quot; PRESENT Feminine &quot;Sailors&quot; Secured Number of Members, Including a Series of Life Memberships Big crowds at Lafontaine Park listened to two series of addresses on behalf of the Navy League last night. It was English-speaking night at the Park, tonight being reserved at the same place for French speakers, the most prominent of whom will be Senators Casgrain and Beaubien<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">The &quot;Scout Ship&quot; last night saifed into the eastern section of the park under command of &quot;Commodores&quot; F. Percy Smith and M. P. Fennell, and manned with a crew of girls, who proved to be experts at capturing members for the league. Ex- Mayor Ekers was chairman at the two meetings<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">There was reason why there should not be 50,000 members from the city of Montreal alone, declared Mr. W. G. M. Shepherd<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">When it was considered what the navy had accomplished for Canada, intense interest should be taken in the project of a Navy League. Canada had been prosperous for four years, and the reason could be traced to British navy, which had enabled counthe try to send its products abroad. Over 400,000 Canadian soldiers had been sent abroad without the loss of a single man because of the British navy. On the banks of the St. Lawrence River the possibilities of building up great mercantile marine were unexcelled, said Mr<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Shepherd, and was not opportunity to be taken of what nature had provided? In Montreal and this province everything was at a hand, including a hardy young manhood. After the war, Canada would have its opportunity for business by having its own ships, and he reminded his hearers of the $90,000,000 programme that the Government had inaugurated. &quot;Wearing the button of the Navy League is a signal mark of honor for all classes and all he declared. There was nothing that should appeal more to the truehearted Canadians than purposes which the Canadian Navy League had at heart. OBJECTS OF THE LEAGUE<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Capt. Frank Symonds spoke of some of the things which the British navy had been able to accomplish. Mr. M. P<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Fennell outlined the varied objects of the Navy League, such as that of having Canadian-built ships, manned by Canadian seamen, and not have the products of Canada, transported from its coasts by Oriental labor. &quot;There are 3,500 people working at the Vickers yards and the Navy League wants ten such shops in declared Mr. F. Percy Smith. Mr<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Smith referred to the aid that Mayor Martin had given the league, and his speech at Sohmer Park urging all to join. CHURCHES IN ENGLAND Closer Relations or Union Considered By the Free Bodies A correspondent in the London Times contributes the following: The &quot;Old Guard&quot; of the Wesleyan Methodists have passed away, and it is no reproach to them that the present leaders, faced with reconstruction in the religious world after the war, are now considering the possibility of tentative steps in the direction of union<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Wider outlook and greater charity have changed the whole conditions, and presentday problems demand the most effective use of men and buildings, higher standard for the training of ministers, lay preachers, and Sunday School teachers, and greater efficiency in organization. Some years ago the Rev. J. H. Shakespeare, secretary of the Baptist Union, proposed a United Free Church of England<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">This idea commerCed itself to many Free Churchmen, out when explored by officially appointed representatives of the various Free Churches in this country the more highly organized bodies were not prepared for such sweeping changes as seemed involved in the suggested unifying of forces. A less ambitious scheme was disbetween providing a Evangelical Free for federal union Churches of England. The Baptists and Congregationalists have agreed to the objects and conditions of such federation, but the Wesleyan Methodists -the largest non -episcopal church in England or Wales have not yet had an opportunity of voting upon the proposals. These are 10 be discussed at the conference to. held at Manchester ir July<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">Many leading Wesleyan Methodists have long desired to prepare the way for Methodist reunion. Methodists agree in doctrine and are only separated by a few differences as to methods of organization. Methodist reunion on a smaller scale has also proved successful, as witness the amalgamation, under the title cf the United Methodist Church, in 1907, of the Methodist New Connexion (founded in 1797), the Bible Christian (1815), and the United Methodist Free Churches (1857), This union has stood the test of ten difficult years, and both those within and those without its membership agree that it made possible the first real and practical step towards the bigger ideal. Even. larger than the United Method<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">1 Church is the&#x27; Primitive Motheist Connexion, many of whose leaders have desired union, but were divided in counsel as to the wisdom of seeking it with the parent body or with the United Methodists. Its conference has discussed the question, taken but in no either practical direction. steps have Primitive Methodists are apparently waiting developments. If the three Methodist churches mentioned were to become a united force, there would exist a membership school of over department 800,000 and a Sunday of over a million and a half of scholars. The possibilities are, therefore, -far-reaching and significant<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">PARADE AT FUNERALS Sinn. Feiners&#x27; Method To Evade Ban on Processions Dublin, June 25-(Correspondence of the Associated that all processions and outdoor meetings have been banned in Dublin, the Sinn Felners have taken to parades at funerals, to which it is obviously difficult and undesirable to apply the prohibition. Sunday is a great day for funerals in all parts of Ireland, and scores of long and picturesque funeral processions may be seen every Sabbath making their way through the Dublin streets, some of them consisting of fifty or more vehicles of all kinds, but principally jaunting cars, each containing five or six friends of the deceased. A great display was made by the Sinn Feiners at the funeral of James Francis Cullen, a young man who took part in the 1916 rebellion. Cullen was sentenced by court martial subsequently to ten years&#x27; penal servitude, commuted to five years, for an active if minor part in the rebellion, and he was released from Lewes jail under the general amnesty in May last year<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">He died from natural causes. His funeral procession included nearly 3,000 members of the Sinn Fein Volunteers, who followed him to his grave in the Fenian Circle in Glasnevin. The procession through the streets drew large crowds of sympathizers. It was wisely ignored by the military and the police. The Sinn Fein paraders, with equal wisdom, refrained from pressing any direct challenge, such as marked the funeral of Thomas Ashe last year when a firing party, following military usage, carried reversed rifles<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">In Cullen&#x27;s funeral procession no arms were seen, and it was not until the rites had been completed at the grave side that a small party produced revolvers and fired a milltary salute. The crowd dispersed quietly, and an event which had given rise to some apprehension passed off with orderliness. Limited 2 Inspector Street KUEHLMANN CRISIS AIDED MILITARISTS His Resignation Triumph For Pan-Germans-Influential Tough Replaces Him Special Cable to the N.Y. Times and Montreal Gazette (Copyright). Paris, July resignation of the Foreign Secretary, Dr. von Kuehlmann, is generally regardea here evidence of the triumph of the pan-Germans, who refuse to forgive him for daring to tell Germany plainly what is beginning to gain greater and greater belief throughout the country, namely, that Germany cannot achieve a victory by force of arms<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">This victory of the military party is interpreted here as foreshadowing a. speedy resumption of the offensive with a desperate determination to stick at no means to bring about the final triumph of the forces which now dominate the world. France is, of course, confident that this final effort is doomed to failure and notes with satisfaction that the effect of Kuehlmann&#x27;s speech in awakening the German people to the real facts must have been considerable or his political adversaries would not have taken such an extreme step as to bring it about. The reported prospective appointment of Admiral von Hintze to succeed Kuehlmann as Foreign Secretary has been received with great interest and not a little amusement Here, where his character and antecedents are well known. According to French&#x27; opinion, Hintze is a highly placed &quot;tough&quot; of the worst description<!-- -->.</p><p style="font-size:1rem;line-height:1.5em">The Journal remarks: &quot;Such a man would be much better suited to lead the Bolshevik than to direct German diplomacy. We shall only have to congratulate ourselves if this, pan-German delirium takes him from his proper post and pushed him into a position where his deficiencies will do them more harm than his very special quality could be used for them in other directions.&quot; Von Hintze, who was a naval officer until his personal friendship for William II, transferred him to diplomacy, is regarded here as a genius for intrigue and adventure, and is classed with Bernstorff, von Papen, Boy-Ed as a ready tool for the execution of any kind of dirty work the Emperor wants done. The French recall that it was Hintze who was sent to Russia 1910 on a confidential mission to try to undermine the influence of France with her ally, the weak -minded Nicholas, and in that he carried some of the letters comprised in the &quot;Willy- -Nicky&quot; correspondence, Hintze&#x27;s work as German minister to Mexico, where he deliberately set himself to bring about a quarrel be- IT IS CONSIDERED BAD FORM to serve your guests with tap water. NO. 165 THE GAZETTE, MONTREAL, THURSDAY, JULY 11, 1918. JAIL FOR POINTING GUN AT PRIEST Man Sentenced Has Also Attempted Robbery Charge To Face CITY AND DISTRICT NEWS Boys Sent to Reformatory For Being Concerned in Stealing Watches From Jewellery Store Joseph Larue, who was arrested in connection with the robbery of a poor box at Loyola College, and who was caught in the bushes after a citizen had disabled him with buckshot, appeared a before Judge Cusson yesterday to answer the charge of pointing a revolver at Rev. Father McLellan, Larue was found guilty and condemned to spend 15 days in jail. He was brought to court yesterday from the hospital at Bordeaux jail, as he is still suffering from wounds in his leg, caused by the buckshot. will face a charge of robbery afterwards. NAVY LEAGUE CONCERT. \u0026quot;The Littlest Girl,\u0026quot; a dramatic offering by Messrs. Walter Cluxton, Robinson, A. W. Leaman and Miss Elmer Bird, was a successful feature last night at the Catholic Sailors\u0026apos; Club weekly entertainment. The sailor talent contributed to by Messrs. Gloyne, Wall, Hearn, dancers; James and Stephen Woods, vocalists, and Alfred Caplin, conjurer. The aims of the Navy League were put before the audience of citizens by Dr. Atherton, and the chairman, Capt. Leo. Ryan, drew special attention to the intention of the Navy League to look after the special needs of the sailors themselves, and of their worthy treatment after the AT CAMP KANAWANA. Camp Kanawana, the Y.M.C.A. outing centre, has the largest attendance this year of any season in its history, 110 members having in camp last week- end. Instruction in first aid work, basketmaking, camp sanitation, wrestling, tumbling and nature study is being carried on. The camp. was visited few days ago and Mrs. Frank Lawes, of London, England, who are touring the world, taking films of Y.M.C.A. work. A reel of the activities at Kanawana is to be added to their collection. Another visitor was Mr. Philip D. Fagans, secretary a and organizer of the Woodcraft League, of New York. He gave a demonstration of the work to the boys in camp. CLEAN-UP WEEK PRIZES. MALICIOUS EXPLOSION. An evident intention to do injury to the inhabitants of the house was the cause leading to an explosion of dynamite in the lower storey of a three-storey tenement at 425 Elm street, in the east end of the city, after 11 o\u0026apos;clock on Tuesday night. Mr. and Mrs. Pauline Saygot occupied the lower flat. The husband, a chauffeur, was out at the time of the explosion, and Mrs. Saygot was awaiting his return. A stick of dynamite had been placed on the window sill, and the explosion wrecked the window and interior of the front room, while Mrs. Saygot was thrown from her chair in the kitchen. Mrs. Saygot told the police of seeing a strange man loitering in the vicinity on Sunday and furnished his description. Detectives are on the case. FREE FERRY FOR CHILDREN. The City Playgrounds Association has arranged that all children up to 13 years of age may go to the picnic arranged at St. Helen\u0026apos;s Island today free of all charge on the terry, Refreshments on sale will be sold cheaper than in the city for the day. Besides this there will be a band, sports, prizes, decorations and gifts. Before the sports bonbons will be distributed free to the children, and in the course of the afternoon rustic dances will be given by little girls from Lafontaine Park district. EDNA ROBINSON APPEARED. Edna Robinson, who has been reporting to Judge Choquet at regular intervals since she was found guilty of contempt of court in connection with the Epstein case, appeared before his Honor again yesterday, Mrs. Robinson said that she was still under the surveillance of Detectives Tierney and Forget, and that she was well protected. Owing to the fact that a charge of perjury had been laid against Mrs. Robinson, and that the Villeneuve-Roberts libel suit was still pending, his Honor ordered her to report to him again on Wednesday next. Pigeons Feel the Pinch London, June pigeons of St. Paul\u0026apos;s are not as fat as they used to be. War rations and airraids have affected he them materially. Visitors to London\u0026apos;s famous cathedral are not as numerous as they were in pre- war days and even those persons who do feed the pigeons now days don\u0026apos;t care to pay twenty-five cents a pint for peanuts just to see the big birds peck. It\u0026apos;s a violation of Defense of the Realm Act to feed bread to birds, so the pigeons have to content themselves principally with scanty leavings from the cab horses\u0026apos; dinner bags. The pigeons of St. Paul\u0026apos;s, and of all London, too, dread the buzz of an airplane propeller overhead and even during the daytime when an observing allied aviator appears in the sky--and this is almost daily--the pigeons flutter about and fret considerably until he is out of sight. And at night, when the Boches have come, dropping bombs and things, the pigeons are out in a jiffy from their roost in the belfry wherein is hung Great Paul of seventeen tons, St. Paul\u0026apos;s largest bell, never returning until daylight. They spend the remainder of the night on adjoining buildings or wherever they happen to alight when the air raid is at ite height. \u0026quot;One could feed those pigeons all the peanuts and wheat they could eat,\u0026quot; said a policeman, whose station is near St. Paul\u0026apos;s Cathedral, recently, \u0026quot;but they\u0026apos;ll never take on any flesh so long a8 there are aviators about. Bombs and the hum of the airplane worry them nearly out of their feathers.\u0026quot; Lake Resorts in Southern B.C. \u0026quot;Lake Resorts in Southern British Columbia\u0026quot; is a new and handsomely illustrated folder just issued by the Canadian Pacific Railway. South of the main line of the C.P.R. through the Rocky Mountains, stretching to the U. S. border, is a wonderful district that is comparatively little known. It is extremely picturesque, its lakes, mountain peaks, fruit orchards and metal mines offering a variety of interest. With the construction of the Kettle Valley Railway, it is now possible to reach Vancouver by this southern route, leaving the main line of the C.P.R. at Medicine Hat, and traversing the Crow\u0026apos;s Nest Pass, Kootenay Lake, passing the Arrow Lakes and Okanagan Lake, and thence to Vancouver through the Coquihalla Canyon. This district, which is well served by both rail and water transportation, 18 becoming a popular holiday resort as well as a different route through to the Pacific Coast; and the C.P.R., in order to give information about the many beautiful places en route, have issued this folder. Amongst the districts described are the Columbia Valley, Kootenay Lake. Nelson, Kaslo, the Arrow Lakes, Nakusp, the Slocan Lake, Okanagan Lake, Penticton. Kelowna, etc. Copies of the folder can be obtained from Mr. F. C. Lydon, City Passenger Agent, 141- 145 St. James Montreal. Watters RAIDS BY POLICE NET 250 PERSONS Surprise Visit Also Resulted in Seizure of 32 Slot Machines CAREFULLY PLANNED Raiding Parties Visited Suspected Premises Simultaneously Search Warrants Used The first 1 big gun in Director Joseph Tremblay\u0026apos;s effort with the Montreal police to clean the city of vice was fired last night when two big raids planned, organized and carried out by the Director of Public Sofetly, the Assistant, Arthur Mann, and Deputy Chief of Police Grandchamps, landed nearly two hundred and fifty men and women in the police net. Both raids were worked on the same plan the men entering all the places on the list at the same time, and on each occasion the police were successful. In the first raid thirtytwo slot machines were seized, and in the second nearly two hundred and fifty men and women were taken. The first raid was timed for 9.30 o\u0026apos;clock, and the list of all the places where slot machines were located had been furnished the leaders, who, with their men, waited for the strikIng of the clock before they entered simultaneously twenty-three clubs, cigar stores and places of amusement. The proprietors of the places had apparently some wind of the affair, and for the most part acted as though surprised, but said that they did not have any machines on their premises. The police, armed with search warrants, scoured the premises and generally machines were brought to light. Some of machines were found at their regular stands, others were discovered in the cellars, storerooms housed some, and one or two machines had been hidden under the roof of the house. The machines, totalling 32, were taken to headquarters and placed in the office of the Director of Public Safety until there was hardly room to move about in the office. The machines, the total value of which is placed at $3,350, contained plenty of money found in the machines. It was stated last night that the machines would be used first as evidence in the court today and will later be destroyed. Only one man was held by the police in the raid, but all the owners and users of the machines were summoned to appear in court on a charge of gambling. The machines are gum vending machines and in most cases there was, the police state, no gum in the machines. The police had received several complaints about the machines lately, and it was these complaints that decided the officials to act so promptly. After a few days of hard work the detectives secured the addresses of all the stores having the machines and these were all raided last night. RAID AT MIDNIGHT. At twelve o\u0026apos;clock, raid of another nature was made in fifteen alleged houses of ill-fame, which cleared nearly 250 prisoners. About seventy-five p.c. of the prisoners were women. The men, as in the previous raid, entered the places at the\u0026apos; same time and prevented the alarm from being raised and the completeness of the raid spoiled. In all of the houses several women and men were found, and all were taken to headquarters. Very few of the prisoners were allowed out on bail and these few were men. Nearly every nationality was represented in the captures. Negroes and a Chinaman were among them. There, were also several soldiers in During the two raids all the patrol waggons of the city were used, in addition to seven automobiles and some twenty cabs. Seventy-five men, who had done duty all day, under captains of the various stations, and the inspectors, took part in the raids, which were said to be the biggest of their kind evor made in Montreal. The organization was perfect and in not a single Instance was there a hitch. The first raid took place at 9.30 and an hour afterwards the machines were all in the headquarters office to be checked up and made ready to produce as evidence in the morning. In the second raid more rigs were wanted and the various waggons had to make several trips. Early this morning the waggons were still arriving with prisoners. The two raids were planned Director Tremblay and, seconded by Assistant Director Mann and Deputy Chief Grandchamps, the work went well. Orders were given to the detectives and the policemen and their officers of the day staff only at 5 o\u0026apos;clock in order to make the raids as complete a surprise as possible. Most of the streets of the Red Light district were visited in the second raid, while in the first various sections of the city were cleaned up. All the prisoners and those summoned will appear in the arraignment court today, charged either with gambling, keeping gambling houses, and being in houses of illfame, or keeping disorderly houses. A quantity of liquor was seized in the second raid. Director of. Publid Safety Joseph Tremblay stated this morning after the second raid that the underworld must now realize that there is a new administration. \u0026quot;The lid is on,\u0026quot; said Mr. Tremblay, \u0026quot;and we will endeavor to keep it on tight.\u0026quot; A Long and Fast Run (Oxbow, Herald.) We have heard tell of people, even in this country, being chased by dog or a bull, but George Robson had an unusual experience one day last week with a rattlesnake. which, for real down right excitement, knocks common everyday occurrences higher than a cocked hat. Space forbids us giving the details of Mr. Robson\u0026apos;s encounter with this venomous reptile, suffice to say that he is not yet fully recovered from the scare he received and the long run he made to escape its poisonous sting. This snake was not seen, but the weird rattle which these reptiles extend in times of charge was quite sufficient for the pursued to make his presence scarce. LIFE ON U.S. TROOPSHIPS Menace Chief Submarine, Men on Board London, June 6-(Correspondence of The Associated Press) Although troopships that bring over American soldiers are 80 well protected that the submarine menace is virtually negligible, submarines throughout the trip are probably the chief subject of conversation. Usually the references to the undersea terror are jocular, but it is apparent that much serious thought is given to U-boats and that they loom large in imagination. This applies to officers as well as to the men. All say frankly they have no desire for a brush with the slinking, enemy craft. The reason for this was neatly put by a major of infantry, who recently landed in England. \u0026quot;Fighting submarines,\u0026quot; he said, \u0026quot;isn\u0026apos;t our game.\u0026quot; In that pithy explanation he summed up the soldiers\u0026apos; attitude exactly. Fighting the submarines isn\u0026apos;t the army\u0026apos;s game, and soldiers can\u0026apos;t play it because they don\u0026apos;t know how. If their ship is attacked there is nothing for them to do except march on deck and prepare to take to the lifeboats. Defensive measures rest with the transport\u0026apos;s naval guns and with the escorting destroyers. They, as the soldier sees it, have all the fun, while the soidier must stand by, eager to fight, but helpless to take a hand. The army officers feel keenly their responsibility in such an unfamiliar situation. It devolves upon them to clear the ship of every man and get them into their proper boats. In order to do this with the greatest celerity and precision, the commanding military officer and his assistants carefully work out their plans before the ship sails. On a large vessel carrying several thousand troops, it is necessary to quarter the men on all decks, some far down in the vessel. The task, then, is to get them all up on the boat deck with the least delay and without confusion. Boat drills begin soon after the ship leaves port. Each man is assigned to a particular boat, and it is highly important that when the troops, in response to the alarm signal, are moving up from the lower decks that there be no interference and congestion on the stairways. The problem presents a 1 number of difficulties, each of which is studied with care. So perfect was the system employed on one big transport. that the 6,000 troops on board could be brought from all parts of the ship to their stations on the upper deck within less than five minutes. When a transport approaches the submarine zone, precautions are increased. All officers and men must wear their life-preservers constantly, and when the ship has got well into the zone, orders are issued for the men to sleep in their clothes. No lights, of course, are shown. To guard against the inadvertent striking of a match, whose flare might reveal the vessel\u0026apos;s presence to a lurking submarine, no one is permitted on deck after dark, with the exception of the ship\u0026apos;s crew. Sentries are posted to see that this order is strictly obeyed. An amusing incident occurred on a huge British transport which was carrying a particularly large number of American soldiers. About nine o\u0026apos;clock one evening, while full speed was being made through the heart of the zone, a sentry noticed a ray of light playing in a small circle on a distant part of the deck which he was guarding. He called another sentry and together they crept toward the point where the light momentarily had appeared. The night was very dark and at first the sentries could see nothing. Then they made out the figure of a man bending over the deck. They immediately seized him and told him he was under arrst. \u0026quot;But I\u0026apos;m the watch officer in command of the ship,\u0026quot; the prisoner exclaimed. \u0026quot;I have to use a flashlight for the work I\u0026apos;m doing here.\u0026quot; However, the sentries had their orders. They were to arrest anybody that showed a light on deck. So their captive protested in vain. The soldiers called their officer of the day. He decided i to turn the prisoner over to the ship\u0026apos;s captain. Up to the bridge the watch officer was taken, and when the captain saw him and heard the details, he almost choked with laughter. It will be a long time before that officer is permitted to forget his arrest on his own ship by American soldiers. ENEMIES OF RUSSIA Bolsheviki and Huns Allied, With Late Mirbach Dictator London Times Cable Service, Copy- right, 1918. Stockholm, July Nyheter publishes today a letter from Terestchenko, former foreign minister in the Kerensky Government, to Burtzeff, the revolutionary leader, now in France, which, although written before Terestchenko left Russia to join his chief in England, throws light on the position and part played by the late Count Mirbach, German representative at Moscow, and the all-powerful influence he had with the Bolshevik Government when his career was so tragically ended. He says: \u0026quot;There reigns now in Moscow a proconsul whose name is Mirbach. Bolsheviki eloquence flows as usual, but ceases immediately at a frown of this gentleman\u0026apos;s brow. Lenine and Trotzky govern Moscow only thanks to him. It would be the easiest thing for the Germans to turn them out, but they know better. The Bolsheviki are more useful to them even than a government composed of their own generals. Is it not a curious fact while friendly Ukraine Germans and Austrians are obliged to keep an army in the rest of Russia, the Germans require no troops at all, thanks to the Bolsheviki, who do all they can for them. Their wishes are carried out promptly as they would be by their own well-disciplined people. Germany will not permit the reorganization of Russia even with her aid until peace is concluded.\u0026quot; After describing at length the present condition of Russia resulting from \u0026quot;fourteen months of revolution and six months of Bolshevik dominion.\u0026quot; the writer concludes that Russia has two enemies, the Bolsheviki and the Germans, and at present they are allied. NAVY LEAGUE HAD TWO BIG MEETINGS Demonstrations For EnglishSpeaking People Held in Lafontaine Park \u0026quot;SCOUT SHIP\u0026quot; PRESENT Feminine \u0026quot;Sailors\u0026quot; Secured Number of Members, Including a Series of Life Memberships Big crowds at Lafontaine Park listened to two series of addresses on behalf of the Navy League last night. It was English-speaking night at the Park, tonight being reserved at the same place for French speakers, the most prominent of whom will be Senators Casgrain and Beaubien. The \u0026quot;Scout Ship\u0026quot; last night saifed into the eastern section of the park under command of \u0026quot;Commodores\u0026quot; F. Percy Smith and M. P. Fennell, and manned with a crew of girls, who proved to be experts at capturing members for the league. Ex- Mayor Ekers was chairman at the two meetings. There was reason why there should not be 50,000 members from the city of Montreal alone, declared Mr. W. G. M. Shepherd. When it was considered what the navy had accomplished for Canada, intense interest should be taken in the project of a Navy League. Canada had been prosperous for four years, and the reason could be traced to British navy, which had enabled counthe try to send its products abroad. Over 400,000 Canadian soldiers had been sent abroad without the loss of a single man because of the British navy. On the banks of the St. Lawrence River the possibilities of building up great mercantile marine were unexcelled, said Mr. Shepherd, and was not opportunity to be taken of what nature had provided? In Montreal and this province everything was at a hand, including a hardy young manhood. After the war, Canada would have its opportunity for business by having its own ships, and he reminded his hearers of the $90,000,000 programme that the Government had inaugurated. \u0026quot;Wearing the button of the Navy League is a signal mark of honor for all classes and all he declared. There was nothing that should appeal more to the truehearted Canadians than purposes which the Canadian Navy League had at heart. OBJECTS OF THE LEAGUE. Capt. Frank Symonds spoke of some of the things which the British navy had been able to accomplish. Mr. M. P. Fennell outlined the varied objects of the Navy League, such as that of having Canadian-built ships, manned by Canadian seamen, and not have the products of Canada, transported from its coasts by Oriental labor. \u0026quot;There are 3,500 people working at the Vickers yards and the Navy League wants ten such shops in declared Mr. F. Percy Smith. Mr. Smith referred to the aid that Mayor Martin had given the league, and his speech at Sohmer Park urging all to join. Three cheers were given by the crowd for His Worship, and the evening was terminated by singing Canada\u0026quot; and \u0026quot;God Save the King.\u0026quot; The crew of girls was in charge of Captain Edna Marshall, while the financial affairs, as has been the case throughout the whole campaign of the special features week, were handled by Miss Blanche Laviolette The other members of the crew last night were the Misses B. Tupling, M. Hume. R. M. Hume, M. Copping, I. Black, G. Hills, G. McGaughan, R. Hills, M. Price, M. Robinson, M. Hills, G. Flanagan, G. Marshall, M. Currie, Helen Currie, of the Canada Steamship Lines offices; and the Misses M. Smythe, M. Bouchard, M. Smallery, M. Doll, E. MacFarlane, L. Barnfield. L. Possnett, M. Townsent, of the Sun Life Assurance Co. offices. After the demonstration at Lafontaine Park, officers and were entertained at the Windsor Hotel, but even then the sailor girls overlooked no opportunities for business, and, in addition to getting a number of ordinary subscriptions, secured life membership subscriptions of $100 each from Messrs. C. J. Smith, Mr. Stith, of Buffalo; W. G. M. Shepherd, E. R. Carrington, and Master Frederick Johnston, through Mr. Farquhar Robertson. CHURCHES IN ENGLAND Closer Relations or Union Considered By the Free Bodies A correspondent in the London Times contributes the following: The \u0026quot;Old Guard\u0026quot; of the Wesleyan Methodists have passed away, and it is no reproach to them that the present leaders, faced with reconstruction in the religious world after the war, are now considering the possibility of tentative steps in the direction of union. Wider outlook and greater charity have changed the whole conditions, and presentday problems demand the most effective use of men and buildings, higher standard for the training of ministers, lay preachers, and Sunday School teachers, and greater efficiency in organization. Some years ago the Rev. J. H. Shakespeare, secretary of the Baptist Union, proposed a United Free Church of England. This idea commerCed itself to many Free Churchmen, out when explored by officially appointed representatives of the various Free Churches in this country the more highly organized bodies were not prepared for such sweeping changes as seemed involved in the suggested unifying of forces. A less ambitious scheme was disbetween providing a Evangelical Free for federal union Churches of England. The Baptists and Congregationalists have agreed to the objects and conditions of such federation, but the Wesleyan Methodists -the largest non -episcopal church in England or Wales have not yet had an opportunity of voting upon the proposals. These are 10 be discussed at the conference to. held at Manchester ir July. Many leading Wesleyan Methodists have long desired to prepare the way for Methodist reunion. Methodists agree in doctrine and are only separated by a few differences as to methods of organization. Methodist reunion on a smaller scale has also proved successful, as witness the amalgamation, under the title cf the United Methodist Church, in 1907, of the Methodist New Connexion (founded in 1797), the Bible Christian (1815), and the United Methodist Free Churches (1857), This union has stood the test of ten difficult years, and both those within and those without its membership agree that it made possible the first real and practical step towards the bigger ideal. Even. larger than the United Method. 1 Church is the\u0026apos; Primitive Motheist Connexion, many of whose leaders have desired union, but were divided in counsel as to the wisdom of seeking it with the parent body or with the United Methodists. Its conference has discussed the question, taken but in no either practical direction. steps have Primitive Methodists are apparently waiting developments. If the three Methodist churches mentioned were to become a united force, there would exist a membership school of over department 800,000 and a Sunday of over a million and a half of scholars. The possibilities are, therefore, -far-reaching and significant. PARADE AT FUNERALS Sinn. Feiners\u0026apos; Method To Evade Ban on Processions Dublin, June 25-(Correspondence of the Associated that all processions and outdoor meetings have been banned in Dublin, the Sinn Felners have taken to parades at funerals, to which it is obviously difficult and undesirable to apply the prohibition. Sunday is a great day for funerals in all parts of Ireland, and scores of long and picturesque funeral processions may be seen every Sabbath making their way through the Dublin streets, some of them consisting of fifty or more vehicles of all kinds, but principally jaunting cars, each containing five or six friends of the deceased. A great display was made by the Sinn Feiners at the funeral of James Francis Cullen, a young man who took part in the 1916 rebellion. Cullen was sentenced by court martial subsequently to ten years\u0026apos; penal servitude, commuted to five years, for an active if minor part in the rebellion, and he was released from Lewes jail under the general amnesty in May last year. He died from natural causes. His funeral procession included nearly 3,000 members of the Sinn Fein Volunteers, who followed him to his grave in the Fenian Circle in Glasnevin. The procession through the streets drew large crowds of sympathizers. It was wisely ignored by the military and the police. The Sinn Fein paraders, with equal wisdom, refrained from pressing any direct challenge, such as marked the funeral of Thomas Ashe last year when a firing party, following military usage, carried reversed rifles. In Cullen\u0026apos;s funeral procession no arms were seen, and it was not until the rites had been completed at the grave side that a small party produced revolvers and fired a milltary salute. The crowd dispersed quietly, and an event which had given rise to some apprehension passed off with orderliness. Limited 2 Inspector Street KUEHLMANN CRISIS AIDED MILITARISTS His Resignation Triumph For Pan-Germans-Influential Tough Replaces Him Special Cable to the N.Y. Times and Montreal Gazette (Copyright). Paris, July resignation of the Foreign Secretary, Dr. von Kuehlmann, is generally regardea here evidence of the triumph of the pan-Germans, who refuse to forgive him for daring to tell Germany plainly what is beginning to gain greater and greater belief throughout the country, namely, that Germany cannot achieve a victory by force of arms. This victory of the military party is interpreted here as foreshadowing a. speedy resumption of the offensive with a desperate determination to stick at no means to bring about the final triumph of the forces which now dominate the world. France is, of course, confident that this final effort is doomed to failure and notes with satisfaction that the effect of Kuehlmann\u0026apos;s speech in awakening the German people to the real facts must have been considerable or his political adversaries would not have taken such an extreme step as to bring it about. The reported prospective appointment of Admiral von Hintze to succeed Kuehlmann as Foreign Secretary has been received with great interest and not a little amusement Here, where his character and antecedents are well known. According to French\u0026apos; opinion, Hintze is a highly placed \u0026quot;tough\u0026quot; of the worst description. The Journal remarks: \u0026quot;Such a man would be much better suited to lead the Bolshevik than to direct German diplomacy. Watters RAIDS BY POLICE NET 250 PERSONS Surprise Visit Also Resulted in Seizure of 32 Slot Machines CAREFULLY PLANNED Raiding Parties Visited Suspected Premises Simultaneously Search Warrants Used The first 1 big gun in Director Joseph Tremblay's effort with the Montreal police to clean the city of vice was fired last night when two big raids planned, organized and carried out by the Director of Public Sofetly, the Assistant, Arthur Mann, and Deputy Chief of Police Grandchamps, landed nearly two hundred and fifty men and women in the police net. Both raids were worked on the same plan the men entering all the places on the list at the same time, and on each occasion the police were successful\",\".\"]}]\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"5c:[\"$\",\"p\",\"29\",{\"style\":{\"fontSize\":\"1rem\",\"lineHeight\":\"1.5em\"},\"children\":[\"In the first raid thirtytwo slot machines were seized, and in the second nearly two hundred and fifty men and women were taken. The first raid was timed for 9.30 o'clock, and the list of all the places where slot machines were located had been furnished the leaders, who, with their men, waited for the strikIng of the clock before they entered simultaneously twenty-three clubs, cigar stores and places of amusement. The proprietors of the places had apparently some wind of the affair, and for the most part acted as though surprised, but said that they did not have any machines on their premises. The police, armed with search warrants, scoured the premises and generally machines were brought to light. Some of machines were found at their regular stands, others were discovered in the cellars, storerooms housed some, and one or two machines had been hidden under the roof of the house\",\".\"]}]\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"5d:[\"$\",\"p\",\"30\",{\"style\":{\"fontSize\":\"1rem\",\"lineHeight\":\"1.5em\"},\"children\":[\"The machines, totalling 32, were taken to headquarters and placed in the office of the Director of Public Safety until there was hardly room to move about in the office. It was stated last night that the machines would be used first as evidence in the court today and will later be destroyed. Only one man was held by the police in the raid, but all the owners and users of the machines were summoned to appear in court on a charge of gambling. We have heard tell of people, even in this country, being chased by dog or a bull, but George Robson had an unusual experience one day last week with a rattlesnake. which, for real down right excitement, knocks common everyday occurrences higher than a cocked hat. Space forbids us giving the details of Mr. Robson's encounter with this venomous reptile, suffice to say that he is not yet fully recovered from the scare he received and the long run he made to escape its poisonous sting. This snake was not seen, but the weird rattle which these reptiles extend in times of charge was quite sufficient for the pursued to make his presence scarce\",\".\"]}]\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"64:[\"$\",\"p\",\"37\",{\"style\":{\"fontSize\":\"1rem\",\"lineHeight\":\"1.5em\"},\"children\":[\"LIFE ON U.S. TROOPSHIPS Menace Chief Submarine, Men on Board London, June 6-(Correspondence of The Associated Press) Although troopships that bring over American soldiers are 80 well protected that the submarine menace is virtually negligible, submarines throughout the trip are probably the chief subject of conversation. Usually the references to the undersea terror are jocular, but it is apparent that much serious thought is given to U-boats and that they loom large in imagination. This applies to officers as well as to the men. All say frankly they have no desire for a brush with the slinking, enemy craft\",\".\"]}]\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"65:[\"$\",\"p\",\"38\",{\"style\":{\"fontSize\":\"1rem\",\"lineHeight\":\"1.5em\"},\"children\":[\"The reason for this was neatly put by a major of infantry, who recently landed in England. \\\"Fighting submarines,\\\" he said, \\\"isn't our game.\\\" In that pithy explanation he summed up the soldiers' attitude exactly. Fighting the submarines isn't the army's game, and soldiers can't play it because they don't know how. If their ship is attacked there is nothing for them to do except march on deck and prepare to take to the lifeboats. Defensive measures rest with the transport's naval guns and with the escorting destroyers\",\".\"]}]\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"66:[\"$\",\"p\",\"39\",{\"style\":{\"fontSize\":\"1rem\",\"lineHeight\":\"1.5em\"},\"children\":[\"They, as the soldier sees it, have all the fun, while the soidier must stand by, eager to fight, but helpless to take a hand. The army officers feel keenly their responsibility in such an unfamiliar situation. It devolves upon them to clear the ship of every man and get them into their proper boats. In order to do this with the greatest celerity and precision, the commanding military officer and his assistants carefully work out their plans before the ship sails. On a large vessel carrying several thousand troops, it is necessary to quarter the men on all decks, some far down in the vessel\",\".\"]}]\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"67:[\"$\",\"p\",\"40\",{\"style\":{\"fontSize\":\"1rem\",\"lineHeight\":\"1.5em\"},\"children\":[\"The task, then, is to get them all up on the boat deck with the least delay and without confusion. Boat drills begin soon after the ship leaves port. Each man is assigned to a particular boat, and it is highly important that when the troops, in response to the alarm signal, are moving up from the lower decks that there be no interference and congestion on the stairways. The problem presents a 1 number of difficulties, each of which is studied with care. So perfect was the system employed on one big transport\",\".\"]}]\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"68:[\"$\",\"p\",\"41\",{\"style\":{\"fontSize\":\"1rem\",\"lineHeight\":\"1.5em\"},\"children\":[\"that the 6,000 troops on board could be brought from all parts of the ship to their stations on the upper deck within less than five minutes. When a transport approaches the submarine zone, precautions are increased. All officers and men must wear their life-preservers constantly, and when the ship has got well into the zone, orders are issued for the men to sleep in their clothes. No lights, of course, are shown. To guard against the inadvertent striking of a match, whose flare might reveal the vessel's presence to a lurking submarine, no one is permitted on deck after dark, with the exception of the ship's crew\",\".\"]}]\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"69:[\"$\",\"p\",\"42\",{\"style\":{\"fontSize\":\"1rem\",\"lineHeight\":\"1.5em\"},\"children\":[\"Sentries are posted to see that this order is strictly obeyed. An amusing incident occurred on a huge British transport which was carrying a particularly large number of American soldiers. About nine o'clock one evening, while full speed was being made through the heart of the zone, a sentry noticed a ray of light playing in a small circle on a distant part of the deck which he was guarding. He called another sentry and together they crept toward the point where the light momentarily had appeared. The night was very dark and at first the sentries could see nothing\",\".\"]}]\n6a:[\"$\",\"p\",\"43\",{\"style\":{\"fontSize\":\"1rem\",\"lineHeight\":\"1.5em\"},\"children\":[\"Then they made out the figure of a man bending over the deck. Feiners' Method To Evade Ban on Processions Dublin, June 25-(Correspondence of the Associated that all processions and outdoor meetings have been banned in Dublin, the Sinn Felners have taken to parades at funerals, to which it is obviously difficult and undesirable to apply the prohibition. Sunday is a great day for funerals in all parts of Ireland, and scores of long and picturesque funeral processions may be seen every Sabbath making their way through the Dublin streets, some of them consisting of fifty or more vehicles of all kinds, but principally jaunting cars, each containing five or six friends of the deceased. A great display was made by the Sinn Feiners at the funeral of James Francis Cullen, a young man who took part in the 1916 rebellion. Cullen was sentenced by court martial subsequently to ten years' penal servitude, commuted to five years, for an active if minor part in the rebellion, and he was released from Lewes jail under the general amnesty in May last year\",\".\"]}]\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"86:[\"$\",\"p\",\"71\",{\"style\":{\"fontSize\":\"1rem\",\"lineHeight\":\"1.5em\"},\"children\":[\"He died from natural causes. JAIL FOR POINTING GUN AT PRIEST Man Sentenced Has Also Attempted Robbery Charge To Face CITY AND DISTRICT NEWS Boys Sent to Reformatory For Being Concerned in Stealing Watches From Jewellery Store Joseph Larue, who was arrested in connection with the robbery of a poor box at Loyola College, and who was caught in the bushes after a citizen had disabled him with buckshot, appeared a before Judge Cusson yesterday to answer the charge of pointing a revolver at Rev. Father McLellan, Larue was found guilty and condemned to spend 15 days in jail. He was brought to court yesterday from the hospital at Bordeaux jail, as he is still suffering from wounds in his leg, caused by the buckshot. will face a charge of robbery afterwards. MALICIOUS EXPLOSION. An evident intention to do injury to the inhabitants of the house was the cause leading to an explosion of dynamite in the lower storey of a three-storey tenement at 425 Elm street, in the east end of the city, after 11 o'clock on Tuesday night. Mr. and Mrs. Pauline Saygot occupied the lower flat. The husband, a chauffeur, was out at the time of the explosion, and Mrs. Saygot was awaiting his return. A stick of dynamite had been placed on the window sill, and the explosion wrecked the window and interior of the front room, while Mrs. Saygot was thrown from her chair in the kitchen. Mrs. Saygot told the police of seeing a strange man loitering in the vicinity on Sunday and furnished his description. Detectives are on the case. FREE FERRY FOR CHILDREN. The City Playgrounds Association has arranged that all children up to 13 years of age may go to the picnic arranged at St. Helen's Island today free of all charge on the terry, Refreshments on sale will be sold cheaper than in the city for the day. Besides this there will be a band, sports, prizes, decorations and gifts. Before the sports bonbons will be distributed free to the children, and in the course of the afternoon rustic dances will be given by little girls from Lafontaine Park district. EDNA ROBINSON APPEARED. Edna Robinson, who has been reporting to Judge Choquet at regular intervals since she was found guilty of contempt of court in connection with the Epstein case, appeared before his Honor again yesterday, Mrs. Robinson said that she was still under the surveillance of Detectives Tierney and Forget, and that she was well protected. Owing to the fact that a charge of perjury had been laid against Mrs. Robinson, and that the Villeneuve-Roberts libel suit was still pending, his Honor ordered her to report to him again on Wednesday next. The woman, according to the police report, lived with a blind man, and it was reported to the morgue that the woman must have been dead several days. The police are investigating. Pigeons Feel the Pinch London, June pigeons of St. Paul's are not as fat as they used to be. War rations and airraids have affected he them materially. Visitors to London's famous cathedral are not as numerous as they were in pre- war days and even those persons who do feed the pigeons now days don't care to pay twenty-five cents a pint for peanuts just to see the big birds peck. It's a violation of Defense of the Realm Act to feed bread to birds, so the pigeons have to content themselves principally with scanty leavings from the cab horses' dinner bags. The pigeons of St. Paul's, and of all London, too, dread the buzz of an airplane propeller overhead and even during the daytime when an observing allied aviator appears in the sky--and this is almost daily--the pigeons flutter about and fret considerably until he is out of sight. And at night, when the Boches have come, dropping bombs and things, the pigeons are out in a jiffy from their roost in the belfry wherein is hung Great Paul of seventeen tons, St. Paul's largest bell, never returning until daylight. They spend the remainder of the night on adjoining buildings or wherever they happen to alight when the air raid is at ite height. \"One could feed those pigeons all the peanuts and wheat they could eat,\" said a policeman, whose station is near St. Paul's Cathedral, recently, \"but they'll never take on any flesh so long a8 there are aviators about. Bombs and the hum of the airplane worry them nearly out of their feathers.\" Lake Resorts in Southern B.C. \"Lake Resorts in Southern British Columbia\" is a new and handsomely illustrated folder just issued by the Canadian Pacific Railway. South of the main line of the C.P.R. through the Rocky Mountains, stretching to the U. S. border, is a wonderful district that is comparatively little known. It is extremely picturesque, its lakes, mountain peaks, fruit orchards and metal mines offering a variety of interest. With the construction of the Kettle Valley Railway, it is now possible to reach Vancouver by this southern route, leaving the main line of the C.P.R. at Medicine Hat, and traversing the Crow's Nest Pass, Kootenay Lake, passing the Arrow Lakes and Okanagan Lake, and thence to Vancouver through the Coquihalla Canyon. This district, which is well served by both rail and water transportation, 18 becoming a popular holiday resort as well as a different route through to the Pacific Coast; and the C.P.R., in order to give information about the many beautiful places en route, have issued this folder. Amongst the districts described are the Columbia Valley, Kootenay Lake. Nelson, Kaslo, the Arrow Lakes, Nakusp, the Slocan Lake, Okanagan Lake, Penticton. Kelowna, etc. Copies of the folder can be obtained from Mr. F. C. Lydon, City Passenger Agent, 141- 145 St. James Montreal.
